docs.title: Welcome to TatiCloud Documentation Hub
docs.text:
Welcome! This site is a growing collection of practical notes for people working with cloud computing and the Linux terminal. Everything here comes from real hands-on work, such as maintaining servers, fixing problems, and writing down what worked so it can be repeated.

For the main website, visit taticloud.com.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
• Linux commands for cloud computing: checking memory, disk space, and logs, managing swap, and keeping a cloud server healthy.
  • Linux Terminal commands you can copy and use: short, tested examples with a note on what each one does.
  • How to write tech docs: creating clear documentation with Markdown and MkDocs.
  • How to publish your docs: building them locally and pushing them to Git so they're available online.

docs.title: Quick start: create your own docs
docs.text:
1. Install MkDocs and create a project

pip install mkdocs
mkdocs new my-docs
cd my-docs

2. Write in Markdown

Add pages as .md files in the docs/ folder and list them in mkdocs.yml:

site_name: My Docs
nav:
  - Home: index.md
  - Check Free Memory: check-memory.md

3. Preview locally

mkdocs serve

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000. The page reloads each time you save.

4. Push your docs to Git

git init
git add .
git commit -m "First version of docs"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/my-docs.git
git push -u origin main

5. Publish the site

mkdocs gh-deploy

Your site will be available at https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/my-docs/.

docs.title: Good practices
docs.text:
• Keep one topic per page, with commands in code blocks.
  • Never publish passwords, tokens, or server IP addresses.
  • Test commands before documenting them, and note anything that needs sudo.

Happy documenting!

docs.title: Linux Commands for Cloud Computing
docs.text: Practical commands for checking memory, disk, and package health on a Linux cloud server (tested on Ubuntu 22.04).

docs.title: Check Free Memory on Virtual Private Server (VPS)
1. Quick overview
docs.text:
free -h

Look at the available column. It shows memory that can be used without swapping, and it matters more than the free column.

docs.title: 2. Check disk space
docs.text:
Low disk space often shows up together with low memory.

df -h /

sudo du -xhd1 /var 2>/dev/null

sudo journalctl --disk-usage
  • df -h / shows total, used, and free space on the main disk.
  • du -xhd1 /var shows which folders under /var use the most space.
  • journalctl --disk-usage shows how much space system logs take.

docs.title: 3. Check swap
docs.text:
swapon --show

No output means no swap is active.

docs.title: 4. Find which processes use the most memory
docs.text:
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head -n 10

Shows the top 10 processes by memory use.

docs.title: 5. Detailed memory info
docs.text:
head -n 5 /proc/meminfo
vmstat 1 5
  • /proc/meminfo shows total, free, and available memory in detail.
  • vmstat 1 5 prints 5 snapshots, one per second. Watch the si and so columns: values above zero mean the system is swapping.

docs.title: 6. Live view
docs.text:
top

Press M to sort by memory and q to quit.

docs.title: 7. Check for stuck package processes
docs.text:
ps aux | grep -E "apt|dpkg"
sudo dpkg --audit
  • The first command lists running package processes.
  • dpkg --audit reports packages that are half-installed or misconfigured. No output means everything is fine.

!!! Warning

Do not kill package processes or delete lock files until you know what they are.
